section.title: A Call to Repentance and Restoration
section.sectionRationale: After the sternest oracle of wrath, the book closes with its gentlest chapter. God Himself puts words of repentance in Israel's mouth, promises to heal their apostasy and love them freely, and paints their restoration in the imagery of dew, lily, and flourishing vine. A closing word of wisdom presses the reader to walk in the right ways of the LORD.
section.thesis: The God whose anger burned against Israel now calls her home, supplies the very words of her confession, and pledges to heal her waywardness and love her freely, so that a people once withered blossoms again under His grace.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to return with true words of repentance; God's promise to heal, love freely, and make His people flourish; and the farewell to idols with a closing word to the wise.

units.label: Return, O Israel, with words of repentance

verses.text: {{shuv|Return}}, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled by your iniquity.
Bring your confessions and return to the LORD. Say to Him: “Take away all our iniquity and receive us graciously, that we may present the fruit of our lips.
Assyria will not save us, nor will we ride on horses. We will never again say, ‘Our gods!’ to the work of our own hands. For in You the fatherless find {{racham|compassion}}.”

units.label: I will heal their apostasy, I will love them freely
units.note: like the dew, the lily, and the vine

verses.text: I will {{rapha|heal}} their {{meshuvah|apostasy}}; I will {{nedavah|freely}} love them, for My anger has turned away from them.
I will be like the dew to Israel; he will blossom like the lily and take root like the cedars of Lebanon.
His shoots will sprout, and his splendor will be like the olive tree, his fragrance like the cedars of Lebanon.
They will return and dwell in his shade; they will grow grain and blossom like the vine. His renown will be like the wine of Lebanon.

units.label: Done with idols, a word to the wise
units.note: the ways of the LORD are right

verses.text: O Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols? It is I who answer and watch over him. I am like a flourishing cypress; your fruit comes from Me.
Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them. For the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them, but the rebellious stumble in them.

shuv.gloss: To turn, to return, to come back. It is the great refrain of Hosea, the word for the repentance Israel refused again and again. Here God commands it warmly, Return, right back to the LORD, and it echoes through the whole chapter as the way home for a wayward people.

racham.gloss: To have compassion, to feel tender mercy; the noun is linked to the word for womb, picturing a parent's yearning love. The confession that in the LORD the fatherless find compassion reaches back to the book's opening, where the child named Not Loved is renamed Loved, and points to the Father's mercy poured out in Christ.

rapha.gloss: To heal, to make whole, to restore. God promises not merely to forgive Israel's turning away but to heal it at the root, curing the very disposition that made her stray, a healing fulfilled in Christ who bears our sins and by whose wounds we are healed.

meshuvah.gloss: Apostasy, backsliding, waywardness; formed from the same root as shuv, it names the turning away that only God can reverse. He pledges to heal their meshuvah, their bent to wander, so that the incurable turning of the human heart is met and undone by grace.

nedavah.gloss: A freewill offering, spontaneous and uncompelled generosity. God says He will love them nedavah, of His own free bounty, not because they have earned it but because His love overflows freely, the very heart of grace poured out without price in Christ.

basic.context: This is the tender close of Hosea. After the harshest chapter of judgment, God turns and calls His people home. Remarkably, He does not wait for Israel to find the right words; He gives them the words to say. Then He answers with the most generous promise in the book: I will heal your wandering, and I will love you freely. He paints their new life with pictures from nature, dew, lily, olive tree, vine, and wine, a withered people blooming again. He renounces the idols for them and ends with a quiet word to the reader: the ways of the LORD are right, so which way will you walk?
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter is an invitation, still open at the end. God supplies the confession, makes the promise, and then in the final verse turns to every reader and asks for a response. Read in the light of the whole book, the healing of apostasy and the free love God pledges are not earned by Israel's words but given by grace, and the New Testament shows this grace flowing through Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: The key word is shuv, to return, the refrain of the whole book, commanded here with warmth. God promises to rapha, heal, their meshuvah, their apostasy, the very turning away that shares the root of shuv. And He will love them nedavah, freely, as a freewill offering, out of sheer generosity. The confession that in Him the fatherless find racham, compassion, reaches back to the renaming of the child Not Loved as Loved.
basic.typology: The words of repentance God places on Israel's lips point to the confession the Spirit works in believers. The healing of apostasy points to Christ, by whose wounds we are healed. The dew, lily, and flourishing vine picture the abundant life Jesus gives, the true vine in whom His people bear fruit. God's free love foreshadows grace poured out without price at the cross.
basic.christ: God's promise, I will heal their apostasy, I will love them freely, is the gospel in seed form, and it comes true in Jesus. On the cross Christ absorbs the anger that Hosea 13 unleashed, so that here God can say My anger has turned away. By His wounds our waywardness is healed, and His love is given freely, not earned. The fruitful imagery finds its center in Jesus, the true vine, in whom His people abide and flourish. The fatherless who find compassion are welcomed as sons and daughters through Him.
basic.god: God is astonishingly gracious. The same LORD who came like a lion in chapter 13 now comes like the dew, gentle and life-giving. He heals rather than merely pardons, and He loves freely rather than grudgingly. Yet He remains holy: the closing verse warns that the rebellious stumble in the very ways where the righteous walk. His mercy is free but not cheap; it calls for a real return.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 13:15 takes up the fruit of our lips as the sacrifice of praise. John 15 shows Christ as the true vine in whom His people bear fruit. 1 Peter 2:24 says by His wounds we are healed. Romans 5:8 declares God's love shown freely while we were still sinners.
basic.oneStory: Hosea ends with a call home. The God whose wrath had blazed now heals apostasy and loves freely, making a withered people bloom. The whole Bible answers this in Christ, in whom God's anger is turned away, our wandering is healed, and His free love makes us flourish like a well-watered garden.

context.literary:
The chapter is shaped as a conversation in three movements, and the speakers change at each turn. In verses 1 to 3 the prophet speaks and then hands the microphone to the people, putting a prayer in their mouths. In verses 4 to 8 the LORD answers in the first person, and the answer is longer than the prayer, as though His reply cannot be contained. Verse 9 steps outside the conversation altogether, and the voice of the book's editor or the prophet addresses whoever will read.

Two devices hold the chapter together. The first is an inclusio on the verb 'stumble.' Verse 1 says Israel has stumbled by her iniquity, and verse 9 says the rebellious stumble in the ways of the LORD while the righteous walk in them. The chapter begins with a fall and ends with the question of which way a reader will walk. The second is the run of images in verses 5 to 7, which are mostly plants, and which are built on the three kinds of Lebanon: the cedar of its roots, the fragrance of its forests, and the wine of its slopes. The verbs move from root to branch to shade to grain, so that the promised life is traced from the ground up.

The chapter is also a deliberate answer to what came before. The dew of verse 5 answers the vanishing dew of Hosea 6:4 and 13:3. The shoots and the vine answer the dried up fountain of 13:15. The idols of verse 8 are renounced in a line that picks up 'Ephraim is joined to idols' from 4:17. The word 'return' that has driven the book, as in 6:1, 11:5 and 12:6, here gets its answer on the lips of God. Even the quiet statement that the fatherless find compassion points back to the names given to Hosea's children in chapters 1 and 2, so that the book ends by undoing its own opening names.
context.historical:
The chapter is most likely spoken in the final years of the northern kingdom, when Israel looked for help from Assyria and Egypt and was about to be swept away by the first. Verse 3 reflects the political habits of the time. Menahem had paid tribute to Assyria for support, 2 Kings 15:19 and 20, Hoshea later turned to Egypt, 2 Kings 17:4, and Hosea 7:11 had mocked the nation as a silly dove flitting between the two. To say 'Assyria will not save us' was to renounce the whole foreign policy of the northern kings.

The mention of horses is not accidental either. Deuteronomy 17:16 told Israel's king not to multiply horses, and the prophets regularly mocked those who relied on them, Isaiah 31:1 and Psalm 20:7. Horses were military hardware. To say 'we will not ride on horses' is to give up trust in armed force.

The call to 'bring your confessions' fits the temple rhythms of the day. Israel had a settled habit of bringing sacrifices, and Hosea 6:6 had said that God desired loyalty rather than sacrifice. Verse 2 therefore asks for words in place of animals. The footnote on this verse notes that the Hebrew reads 'that we may present our lips as sacrificial bulls,' while the Septuagint and Syriac read 'fruit of our lips.' Both express the idea that praise and confession replace the offering, and the Septuagint wording is the one that the letter to the Hebrews picks up.

The images of the second half would have rung true in a land where fertility was the great issue. Baal was the god who gave dew, grain and wine, so to promise dew, blossoms and wine from the LORD is to claim the very gifts the people had sought from Baal. The Lebanon ranges to the north were famous for cedar and for their wine, and Solomon's love poetry, Song of Songs 4:11, praises the fragrance of Lebanon. The people would have recognised the pictures as pictures of abundance.
context.canonical:
Chapter 14 looks back to the Torah and forward to the new covenant. Its repentance formula, 'take away all our iniquity,' echoes the language of Exodus 34:6 and 7, where the LORD describes Himself as one who forgives iniquity, so that the people pray the divine self-description back to God. The promise that He will heal their turning away answers the pattern of Leviticus 26:40 to 45 and Deuteronomy 30:1 to 6, where exile ends when the people turn back and God circumcises their hearts. Jeremiah 3:22 repeats Hosea's offer almost word for word, 'Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness,' and Jeremiah 3:22 goes on to give the people the reply, 'Here we are. We come to You, for You are the LORD our God.'

The imagery of dew and vine runs on through the prophets. Isaiah 27:2 to 6 speaks of the vineyard of the LORD that will blossom and fill the world with fruit, and Micah 5:7 compares the remnant to dew from the LORD. Psalm 133:3 says that blessing falls like the dew of Hermon. The closing wisdom call has a clear parallel in Psalm 107:43, 'Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD,' and in the two ways of Psalm 1.

In the New Testament Hosea's book as a whole is quoted for the calling of the Gentiles, Romans 9:25 and 26 and 1 Peter 2:10, where those who were 'not a people' become the people of God. Chapter 14's promise that the fatherless find compassion stands under those quotations. Hebrews 13:15 takes the call to offer the 'fruit of lips' and turns it into the believer's continual sacrifice of praise through Jesus. And Jesus' words in John 15:1 to 5 about the vine and the fruit bear a deep connection to verses 6 to 8, since there too fruit comes only from Him.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hosea closes his book with an offer that he expects to be heard before the disaster, not only after it. The first hearers were in the last days of a nation in decline, and the chapter says that the road back is still open. He wants them to see that repentance is not a bargain. The words that Israel is given to say contain no promise of reform and no list of sacrifices, only a plea for pardon and a renunciation of the three props they had leaned on: foreign power, military strength and idols.

He also wants them to see that God's answer outruns their request. They ask to be forgiven and received, and God promises to heal them and love them and make them flourish. The pattern teaches that when a person comes back, what he receives is out of proportion to what he brings. The chapter thus works against the despair that says it is too late and against the pride that says Israel can fix the problem herself.

The final verse is a deliberate turn to the reader. It says that the book is not just a record of what happened to one nation but a test. The wise person is the one who reads the whole thing, the lover and the lion, the hard chapters and the tender ones, and concludes that the ways of the LORD are right. Hosea's intent was that his readers would not shelter in the thought that judgment was for others, and that they would choose which of the two kinds of walkers to be.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The words in verses 2 and 3 are prescribed for Israel in the sense that God puts them on the people's lips, so they are an invitation and a model rather than a magic formula. A believer reading them is not meant to recite the exact words as a rite, but to see the shape of honest repentance: confession of iniquity, request for mercy, renunciation of false saviors, and appeal to the character of God. The prayer has no excuses, no bargaining and no promise of improvement as a condition of forgiveness.

The promises of verses 4 to 7 are descriptive of what God will do for a restored Israel. They are not a guarantee that every repentant person will see instant material blessing, and the pictures of blossom and wine should not be turned into a prosperity pledge. In the New Testament the fulfilment is spiritual first, with the believer growing in Christ, and physical only in the age to come, Romans 8:21. The imagery speaks of life flowing from God, not a deal for good harvests.

The last verse is plain instruction and applies directly. Hosea says that the person who is wise will understand and walk in the right way. It is both a promise and a warning, and it is meant for every reader in every age. The word 'stumble' is a reminder that the same road can be the path of life or the occasion of falling, depending on the heart that walks it.

debates.question: Whose shade do the returning people dwell in, verse 7?

views.label: Israel's own shade, the tree that grows
views.case: The BSB reads 'They will return and dwell in his shade,' following the near context of verses 5 and 6, where Israel is pictured as the lily, the cedar and the olive with their shoots and fragrance. On this reading the restored nation becomes so full of life that its people, who had been scattered, come back and shelter under its branches.

views.label: God's shade, the protecting LORD
views.case: Others take the shade as that of God Himself, who is like the dew in verse 5 and like the flourishing cypress in verse 8, where fruit comes from Him. The shade is the shelter of the LORD, a common picture of protection, as in Psalm 91:1 and Psalm 121:5. In that case the people dwell under the protection of the God who answers.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: Because the passage's whole point is that Israel's life is the life of God given to them, the two meanings need not be separated. The shade is the shelter that flows from the LORD and is seen in the people who have been healed.

debates.bearing: The grammar allows more than one reading, and the translation chooses one. Verse 8 helps a little, because the LORD says 'your fruit comes from Me,' so that even where the tree is Ephraim's, the life in it is borrowed from God. A reader can hold the picture loosely and take the main point, which is that a people who come back find shelter and growth.

debates.question: What do the verbs in verse 8 claim, 'I answer and watch over him'?

views.label: A plain statement of care
views.case: The LORD simply says He is the One who answers prayer and keeps watch. In context, that stands against the idols, who cannot answer. The line answers the request of verse 2 and the renunciation of idols in verse 3.

views.label: A deliberate counter to the Canaanite goddesses
views.case: Some scholars have heard in the two verbs a reply to the names of Anath and Asherah, so that God is claiming the very roles the Baal cult assigned to those goddesses. The proposal is debated, and the verse reads well without it. If it is right, God is saying that everything the fertility religion promised Israel is found only in Him.

debates.bearing: The plain reading is secure, and the proposal about the goddesses, if accepted, adds weight without changing the point. In both cases the claim is exclusive: the answering, watching and fruit-giving all come from the LORD, which is why He asks what He has to do with idols.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with 'stumble,' the verb kashal, which opens and closes the chapter. In verse 1 Israel has 'stumbled by your iniquity,' and in verse 9 the rebellious 'stumble' in the ways of the LORD while the righteous walk in them. It is a word for tripping, a fall on a road, and the same verb is used for the staggering of priest and prophet in Hosea 4:5 and 5:5. The only difference between the two groups in verse 9 is in the person, not the path. The same road is the cause of stumbling for one and of walking for another.

The request 'take away all our iniquity' in verse 2 is, in Hebrew, a phrase with two verbs, literally 'lift up iniquity' and 'take good.' The first uses nasa, to lift or carry, which is the verb used of the LORD in Exodus 34:7 where He is said to forgive iniquity. The second asks God to 'take good,' that is, to receive what is good, and the BSB renders 'receive us graciously.' The prayer asks God to carry the weight away and to accept what is offered. It also pictures forgiveness as a lifting, which is why the Old Testament speaks of a scapegoat that bears away guilt, Leviticus 16:22.

The phrase 'fruit of our lips' is where the textual note matters. The Hebrew text as it stands has 'bulls of our lips,' and the Septuagint and Syriac have 'fruit of our lips.' Either way the idea is that words stand in for the sacrifice, and the epistle to the Hebrews uses the Greek wording when it speaks of 'the fruit of lips that confess His name,' Hebrews 13:15.

In verse 3 the people say 'Assyria will not save us,' and the verb for 'save' is the same root, yasha, that gave the name Jesus and that God claimed for Himself in 13:4. The saving verb that had been placed on Assyria is now taken back from her. The next phrase, 'nor will we ride on horses,' picks up the warnings against cavalry in Deuteronomy 17:16.

The wordplay in verse 4 is the heart of the chapter. God says He will heal their turning away, using the root shuv for the noun meshuvah, and then says 'My anger has turned away from them,' using the verb shav, from the same root. They are called to turn back, and He says that His anger has turned. The same verb is used on both sides of the relationship, and the grammar shows the exchange that the gospel will later spell out.

In verse 8 God says He is 'like a flourishing cypress.' The word for flourishing, ra'anan, means fresh and green, and it is the very word used in the law and the histories for the 'green tree' under which the idolaters worshipped, Deuteronomy 12:2 and 1 Kings 14:23. Israel was seeking life from every green tree, and the LORD claims to be the green tree. The footnote mentions that the tree could also be a pine, juniper or fir, and the fruit that comes from it is the sign that real life comes from Him.

Finally, the two words in verse 9, 'wise' and 'discerning,' chakam and navon, belong to the vocabulary of Proverbs. The wise person is the one who understands that the ways of the LORD are 'right,' yashar, which means straight or level. The book of Hosea, which has run through poetry and judgment, ends with the language of the wisdom school.

typology.type: The dew that falls on Israel, Hosea 14:5
typology.fulfillment: God says He will be like the dew to Israel, so that the withered nation blossoms. In the Old Testament dew is the gift of life in a dry land, and it is the picture of the quiet, unseen coming of God's blessing, Psalm 133:3. In Christ the picture is taken up in His own coming. He comes down quietly, and He says of the Spirit that He gives living water, John 7:37 to 39. Isaiah 26:19 says the dew of the dawn will give birth to the dead. The type falls short because dew evaporates by midday, as Hosea 6:4 complained, while Christ's gift of the Spirit is a spring that does not fail.

typology.type: The healing of the wayward, Hosea 14:4
typology.fulfillment: God promises to heal the apostasy, treating unfaithfulness as a sickness. The prophets had said the same of a nation that was wounded from head to foot, Isaiah 1:5 and 6, and the hope was that the LORD would bind up the wound. In Christ the metaphor becomes literal and deeper. Isaiah 53:5 says 'by His stripes we are healed,' and Peter quotes it, 1 Peter 2:24, saying that He bore our sins in His body on the tree. The correspondence is that the healer takes the sickness on Himself. The type falls short in that Israel's healing was a promise in words, while Christ paid for it.

typology.type: The fruitful vine and the one who bears the fruit, Hosea 14:6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: Israel is pictured as a vine and a planted tree whose fruit comes from the LORD. Israel was often called the LORD's vine, Psalm 80:8 and Isaiah 5:1 to 7, and she kept producing wild grapes. In Christ the vine appears again, with a decisive change: 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1, and His people bear fruit only by remaining in Him, John 15:4 and 5. He is the faithful Israel who yields what God was looking for. The type falls short because Israel's fruit was always a gift and was lost when she turned away, while those who abide in the true vine are promised that their fruit will remain, John 15:16.

typology.type: The fatherless who find compassion, Hosea 14:3
typology.fulfillment: The prayer says that in the LORD the fatherless find compassion. Israel in exile was in the position of the orphan, with no one to protect her, and the LORD in the law is the defender of the fatherless, Psalm 68:5. In Christ the orphan is adopted. Paul says believers receive 'the Spirit of adoption' and cry 'Abba, Father,' Romans 8:15, and Jesus says 'I will not leave you as orphans,' John 14:18. Hosea's own children were named Not Loved and Not My People, and Paul and Peter apply the reversal to Gentiles as well as Jews, Romans 9:25 and 1 Peter 2:10. The type falls short only in being less than the reality: Israel was shown compassion, and believers are given sonship.

study.christ:
The chapter begins to lead to Christ with the quiet fact that God supplies the words. Israel is told to say 'take away all our iniquity,' but she has no way of making that prayer come true. A prayer for iniquity to be carried away needs someone to carry it. John the Baptist names Him, 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, picking up the picture of a sin carried away. The request Hosea hands to the people is fulfilled in the person who stands where the scapegoat stood.

It leads to Christ by the promise of healing. The LORD says 'I will heal their apostasy,' and the New Testament says how. Isaiah 53:5 says that by His wounds we are healed, and Peter takes it as a statement about sin and righteousness, not merely sickness, 1 Peter 2:24. The healing Hosea promises is the cure of a turned back heart, and that is exactly what the gospel offers. Jeremiah 3:22 repeats the offer, 'I will heal your faithlessness,' and the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:33 to 34 gives the means, a law written on the heart and sins remembered no more.

It leads to Christ by the free love of verse 4. God does not say that He will love them once they have earned it, but that He will love them freely, and the stated reason is that His anger has turned away. Paul sees the structure in Romans 5:8 to 10, where God shows His love in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us, and where we are reconciled to Him while we are enemies. Romans 3:25 says that God put Christ forward as a propitiation, so that the anger which Hosea 13 describes is turned away by a sacrifice and not by a mood. The reason Hosea can say 'My anger has turned' after chapter 13 is that the anger has found its object in a substitute. Said carefully, Hosea does not yet see the cross, but the shape of the New Testament's account is already in his sentence.

It leads to Christ by the vine. Israel's fruit is said to come from the LORD, verse 8, and Jesus takes the language into His own mouth when He says, 'I am the vine; you are the branches. If you remain in Me and I in you, you will bear much fruit; apart from Me you can do nothing,' John 15:5. The imagery of abundance, of dew, lily, olive and wine, is tied in the gospel to a person. At Cana the water becomes wine, John 2:1 to 11, and at the table the cup is the blood of the new covenant, Luke 22:20.

And it leads to Christ by the family language. The fatherless find compassion, and Hosea's own children had been named for the withdrawal of it. Paul says the same children have been made sons, and Peter says those who once had not received mercy have now received mercy, 1 Peter 2:10. The adoption of the orphan is the gospel in a sentence.

A caution is in order. The dew, the lily and the cedar are poetic images of Israel's restoration, and it would be a mistake to look for a hidden Christ in every plant. The links that stand are those the New Testament itself makes: healing, anger turned away, free love, fruit that comes from God, and adoption.
study.god:
The chapter shows the LORD as the God who goes first. Israel is told to return, but the next sentence is that God has already put words in her mouth, and the sentence after that is that His anger has already turned. This is not a God who waits behind arms folded for the right apology. It is the same Father who in Luke 15:20 runs to the prodigal while he is still a long way off. In Hosea, the repentance that God asks for is made possible by the God who asks.

It shows the LORD as the one who changes the metaphor without changing His character. In chapter 13 He is the lion, the leopard and the bear, and here He is the dew, the cypress and the shelter. The difference is that Israel has stopped being a prey and has come under His care. The terrible and the tender belong to a single holiness, and what decides which a person meets is whether he is fleeing the LORD or returning to Him. Nothing in the chapter suggests that God has softened as a person. His anger had a reason, and when that reason is dealt with it has gone.

It shows a God who loves freely. The word the text uses means a freewill gift, something given because the giver wishes to give. That cuts against every religion that treats a god as a creditor. The statement that He loves them freely is deeply connected to His self-description in Exodus 34:6, that He is abounding in loving devotion, and to Hosea 11:8 and 9, where He says He will not execute the full fury of His anger, for He is God and not man.

It shows a God who is jealous in a gracious way. 'What have I to do anymore with idols?' is the question of a husband who has taken back a wife and no longer wants to hear about the lovers. Idols had never given anything to Ephraim, and He asks His people to see that every good gift they enjoyed was from Him, as James 1:17 says. The cypress that shelters them is God Himself.

It shows a God who teaches. The last verse moves from address to wisdom, and implies that God wants understanding as well as obedience. The ways of the LORD are right, and the final line holds mercy and warning in one verse: the same path is the road of life for the righteous and the place of stumbling for the rebellious. That is the judgment of the whole book, put in a single line.

For worship, the chapter gives believers a script for approaching God after failure. We come with words, not with a plan. We name our false saviors, as Israel names Assyria, horses and idols, and we plead the character of God, who has compassion on the fatherless. And we are meant to rise from prayer expecting to find dew, not a lion, because the God who is the same yesterday and today has promised to turn from His anger to those who come to Him.

crossReferences.note: 'Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness.' This is the same offer in the same words, using the same root for turning and for faithlessness, and the people's reply follows at once, 'Here we are. We come to You.' Jeremiah shows that Hosea's call was not a one-off but a standing invitation.

The earlier call, 'Come, let us return to the LORD, for He has torn us, but He will heal us.' In chapter 6 the people's repentance was shallow, and verse 4 said their loyalty was a vanishing mist. Hosea 14 returns to the theme with words that God Himself dictates, and with a promise that does not vanish.

God's heart is turned within Him and He will not execute the full fury of His anger, for He is God and not man. These words are the root of the promise in 14:4 that His anger has turned away. The reason for the change is who He is, not what Israel has done.

The LORD's self-description, compassionate and gracious, abounding in loving devotion, forgiving iniquity. The prayer 'take away all our iniquity' in Hosea 14:2 pleads that self-description, so that Israel asks God to be what He has said He is.

'Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.' This is Hosea 14:2 in its Greek wording, applied to believers. The sacrifice is words of confession and praise, offered through the one mediator.

God complained that Israel's loyalty was like the early dew that vanishes. In Hosea 14:5 the LORD says He Himself will be like the dew to Israel. What Israel could not sustain, God provides, and what vanished from her hands will not vanish from His.

Paul quotes Hosea's reversal of the children's names, 'I will call them My people who are not My people,' and applies it to the calling of Gentiles. The compassion promised to the fatherless in Hosea 14:3 reaches wider than Israel, and Paul sees the gospel in the prophet's words.

Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy. Peter draws on Hosea's names to show that the mercy promised to the fatherless has come through Christ.

Jesus says 'I am the true vine' and 'apart from Me you can do nothing.' Hosea 14:8 says 'your fruit comes from Me.' The two verses state the same truth, that the fruit of the people of God is the gift of God, and Jesus makes Himself the source.

'Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD.' The call to be wise at the end of Hosea belongs to the same tradition, in which understanding the deeds of the LORD is the beginning of a right life.

The king must not multiply horses. Hosea 14:3 has the people renounce horses, which means they are returning to the Torah's own terms for how Israel should be governed, with trust in the LORD in place of cavalry.

When the people return to the LORD their God, He will gather them and circumcise their hearts. This is the Torah's promise of what God will do after exile, and Hosea 14 shows the prophet's version of the same hope, with the healing coming from God.

study.oneStory:
Chapter 14 is where the prophet answers a question the story has been carrying since Eden: after a people has rebelled, is there a road back? In Genesis 3 God comes looking for the hiding pair and asks 'Where are you?' Here, at the end of Hosea, the same God tells the hiding people to come, hands them the words, and promises more than they dare ask. The whole book has been a marriage story, in which a faithful husband takes back an unfaithful wife, and the final chapter is the reconciliation.

What it answers from before is the long run of broken covenant. Israel had been warned in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 that rebellion would end in exile, and Deuteronomy 30 had said that if they returned, the LORD would restore them. Hosea says that this restoration is not a distant possibility but the very thing God longs to do. The chapter rests on the character of God as given in Exodus 34, where mercy comes before judgment in the list of what He is.

What it sets up is the promise of a new covenant. Jeremiah takes Hosea's pattern into the promise of a covenant written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34. Ezekiel pictures the dry land becoming like Eden, Ezekiel 36:35, and speaks of a spirit put within, Ezekiel 36:26 and 27. The northern tribes were scattered by Assyria, but the promise that the dew would fall on Israel was not cancelled. The prophets carry the hope across the exile and look for a day when God's people, from north and south, are brought together under one shepherd, Ezekiel 37:24.

The story comes to rest in Christ, who is the one in whom God's anger is turned away and in whom the healing of apostasy is accomplished. Paul says that God has reconciled us to Himself through Christ, and that He has given us the ministry of reconciliation, 2 Corinthians 5:18 to 20, which is Hosea's plea to return, now made by the church to the world. The fatherless are brought into the family, the wild branches are grafted into the olive tree, Romans 11:17, and the vine bears fruit.

The new creation is where dew, lily and vine are no longer metaphors. John sees a river of the water of life and the tree of life bearing fruit every month, Revelation 22:1 and 2, with the leaves for the healing of the nations. The healing that Hosea promised to apostasy is carried to the whole world. The people who had stumbled are given a place to walk, and the last wise saying of the prophet, that the ways of the LORD are right, is found true to the end.

sermon.title: The Way Home: An Exposition of Hosea 14
sermon.why: Kidner walks verse by verse through Hosea 14 as the way home, showing how God supplies the words of repentance, heals apostasy, loves freely, and presses the closing appeal on every reader, drawing out the grace of the chapter for the soul's good.

quiz.q: What is striking about the repentance God calls for in verses 1 to 2?

options.text: God Himself supplies the very words of confession His people are to bring to Him.
options.note: God gives Israel the words to say, Take away all our iniquity, so even repentance is a gift of grace.

options.text: God demands only more sacrifices of flocks and herds.
options.note: The chapter asks for the fruit of the lips and a returning heart, not mere sacrifices.

options.text: God requires Israel to save herself before He will listen.
options.note: Israel renounces self-help; salvation comes from God, not Assyria or horses or their own hands.

options.text: God refuses to hear any confession at all.
options.note: Far from refusing, God invites the confession and even provides its words.

quiz.q: What does God promise in verse 4?

options.text: To heal their apostasy and love them freely, for His anger has turned away.
options.note: Verse 4 is the heart of the chapter, free healing and free love.

options.text: To love them only if they first prove themselves worthy.
options.note: The love is nedavah, freely given, not earned.

options.text: To forgive them but keep His anger burning against them.
options.note: God says plainly that His anger has turned away from them.

options.text: To abandon them permanently for their idolatry.
options.note: The verse promises restoration, not abandonment.

quiz.q: What do the images of dew, lily, olive, and vine picture?

options.text: A withered people restored to fresh, rooted, fruitful life under God's grace.
options.note: The nature imagery pictures Israel revived, stable, and flourishing.

options.text: The coming judgment of drought and famine.
options.note: These are images of blessing and life, not judgment.

options.text: The wealth Israel gained from idols.
options.note: The fruit comes from God, verse 8, not from idols.

options.text: Nothing in particular; they are only decoration.
options.note: The imagery deliberately portrays restoration and flourishing.

quiz.q: How does the promise to heal apostasy and love freely point to Christ?

options.text: In Christ God's anger is turned away and borne at the cross, so He freely heals our wandering and gives free love.
options.note: Christ absorbs the wrath so the free healing and love of verse 4 are secured.

options.text: It means believers will never wander or struggle again in this life.
options.note: It means the root of wandering is being healed, not that the struggle instantly vanishes.

options.text: It refers only to rescue from the Assyrian army.
options.note: The healing reaches the heart's apostasy, far beyond political rescue.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ.
options.note: The free healing and love are fulfilled in Christ, by whose wounds we are healed.

quiz.q: What is the point of the closing verse, that the ways of the LORD are right?

options.text: It presses every reader to respond, for the righteous walk in God's ways while the rebellious stumble in them.
options.note: Verse 9 turns the whole prophecy into a personal call to choose the right way.

options.text: It teaches that God's ways are too mysterious to follow.
options.note: The verse says the wise can understand and walk in them.

options.text: It says everyone automatically walks the right way.
options.note: The rebellious stumble; the response is not automatic.

options.text: It cancels the call to repentance in the rest of the chapter.
options.note: It seals the call, pressing the reader to walk in God's ways.

questions: God gave Israel the very words of their confession. How does it help you to know that even your repentance is met and enabled by God's grace?
Israel had to renounce Assyria, horses, and the work of their own hands. What false hopes or self-made securities do you need to let go of to trust God alone?
God promises to heal apostasy, not just forgive it. Where do you long for God to heal the root of your wandering, and not only pardon its fruit?
God says He will love His people freely, out of His own bounty. How does free love, love you cannot earn, change the way you come to Him?
The chapter ends by asking which way you will walk. What would it look like this week to walk in the right ways of the LORD rather than stumble in them?

translationNotes.note: That we may present the fruit of our lips follows the Septuagint and Syriac; the Hebrew reads that we may present our lips as bulls, that is, as sacrificial offerings. Hebrews 13:15 takes up the fruit of the lips as the sacrifice of praise.
Take root like the cedars of Lebanon renders the Hebrew, which reads Lebanon; some modern versions conjecture poplar for the striking picture of a tree taking root.
I am like a flourishing cypress may also be rendered pine, juniper, or fir. The speaker is debated, but the sense is that God alone is the living source from whom all true fruit comes.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Hosea 14:1-9, with poetic lines joined into running verses.
